company.name: Mercadito
company.pitch: A marketplace for neighbourhood sellers, with payments. Three founders, one database, a launch date.
company.role: You were hired as the architect. It is your first day and your first drawing.

company.ordersGrowthYear1: After launch, orders roughly double every quarter in Year 1. Typical of a marketplace finding its first cities; nobody promised it.
company.ordersGrowthYear2: Year 2 growth slows to about 60% a quarter as the easy neighbourhoods run out.
company.ordersGrowthYear3: Year 3 grows about 35% a quarter: a business now, not a rocket.
company.hiringYear1: One engineer joins per quarter in Year 1. Hiring is slow when nobody has heard of you.
company.hiringYear2: Four engineers a quarter in Year 2, after the seed round.
company.hiringYear3: About fourteen engineers a quarter in Year 3, to reach roughly 80 by the end.
company.featureSediment: Every quarter of features leaves a little accidental complexity behind, whatever the architecture.
company.coordinationCost: Past about 20 people, communication paths grow faster than headcount; every quarter adds coordination load.
company.burn: The company burns about three months of runway per quarter until revenue catches up.
company.demandNoise: Demand varies quarter to quarter by up to 6%, for reasons no architecture controls.
company.congestion: A component running past its capacity shows up as incidents: timeouts, retries, angry Fridays.
company.revenueDilution: Revenue grows faster than spend, so each quarter the same bills weigh a little less.
company.operationalLearning: Each quarter's incidents leave runbooks, alerts and habits behind; reliability improves a little even if nothing else changes.

reversibility.hostedShipsFast: A hosted checkout is days of integration, not weeks. Easy to undo: you can always build your own later.
reversibility.hostedRunsHardPart: The vendor runs card storage, fraud checks and compliance, which are hard to get right with three people.
reversibility.hostedUxCeiling: Every checkout UX change becomes a support ticket to the vendor: their page, their flow.
reversibility.hostedFeeScales: The fee is a percentage of every order. It is cheap at 40 orders a day and noticeable at 400.
reversibility.hostedOutageIsYours: When the vendor's checkout goes down, nobody can pay, and there is no fallback to switch to.
reversibility.portCostsAWeek: A port with one adapter costs about one engineer-week before launch, out of six.
reversibility.portOneImplementation: An interface with exactly one implementation is an abstraction you pay for before it pays you.
reversibility.portEngineeringTime: The week spent on the port is a week of three salaries not spent on features.
reversibility.portNewConcept: One more concept to learn: where payments live and how the port is meant to be used.
reversibility.portTestedSeam: A clear seam makes payments testable in isolation; checkout regressions drop.
reversibility.portOutageNoFallback: The port could take a second processor, but only one adapter exists. During an outage, the door is there and the corridor is not.
reversibility.serviceEatsRunway: Building a payments service, its ledger and its deploys takes the whole six weeks for three people.
reversibility.serviceDistributed: Two deployables, a network call, a queue and two databases: distributed systems complexity on day one.
reversibility.serviceInfrastructure: A second database, a queue and their environments, paid from the first month.
reversibility.serviceNewFailureModes: Network calls fail, queues back up, events arrive twice. New failure modes before there is traffic to justify them.
reversibility.serviceTwoSystems: Three people now carry two systems in their heads, plus the contract between them.
reversibility.serviceDelaysLaunch: Launch slips by about six weeks: roughly two months of runway spent with no revenue.
reversibility.servicePciScope: Handling card data directly puts the company in PCI DSS scope: audits, controls, and the people to run them.
reversibility.serviceQueuesThroughOutage: With an own ledger and a queue, orders can be accepted and settled after the network recovers.
reversibility.outageRefunds: A two-hour processor outage on a Saturday: refunds, apologies, a little lost trust.
reversibility.fridayPeak: Friday evening traffic runs about three times the daily average. The monolith notices first.
reversibility.hostedPriceChange: At renewal the hosted checkout reprices its fee; leaving means rebuilding checkout, so the increase gets signed.
reversibility.hostedAuditScope: Card data never touches our systems, so most payment controls are the vendor's to evidence.
reversibility.hostedBlackFridayFee: A percentage fee scales with the spike: the best sales week is also the most expensive one.
reversibility.portPriceChange: The processor raises its price, but the port makes a second adapter credible, so the increase is negotiable.
reversibility.portReservoirDry: Payments still write to the shared Postgres, so when it runs dry checkout waits with everyone else.
reversibility.servicePriceChange: A direct card-network link has no processor margin to reprice; interchange is set by the networks, not at a vendor's renewal.
reversibility.serviceAuditScope: An own ledger and direct card handling put us fully in audit scope: access reviews, key management and reconciliation evidence are all ours.
reversibility.serviceBlackFridayBuffer: The payment-events queue absorbs the checkout burst instead of passing it straight to the card network.
reversibility.serviceKeyEngineer: Ledger knowledge from the three-person era leaves with the person who wrote it.
reversibility.serviceReservoirDry: Payments keep their own reservoir, so a dry shared Postgres does not stop money moving.
reversibility.serviceLicenceScope: A licensed company that runs its own ledger must evidence every control around it to the regulator.

sources.fsa: Architecture characteristics, trade-off analysis, and why everything in architecture is a trade-off.
sources.hardParts: Granularity, data ownership and the forces that pull services apart or together.
sources.apsd: Deep modules, information hiding, and complexity as the sum of dependencies and obscurity.
sources.boringTech: Innovation tokens: spend novelty only where it buys you something.
sources.teamTopologies: Cognitive load as a design constraint; team shapes and interaction modes.
sources.evolutionary: Fitness functions: automated checks that keep an architecture honest as it changes.
sources.nygardAdr: The ADR format: context, decision, status, consequences. Short, versioned, kept with the code.
sources.bezosDoors: Type 1 (one-way door) and Type 2 (two-way door) decisions, and why they deserve different speeds.
sources.lrm: Decide at the last responsible moment: late enough to know more, early enough to still act.
sources.conway: Systems tend to mirror the communication structure of the organisations that build them.
sources.brooks: Essential complexity belongs to the problem; accidental complexity is the one we add.
sources.monolithFirst: Start with a monolith and split once the boundaries are understood.
sources.tilkov: The counterpoint: splitting a monolith later is so hard that you may want to start with boundaries.
sources.ddia: Replication, partitioning, consistency models and the trade-offs between them.
sources.cap: The CAP theorem revisited: the real choice is about what to do during a partition.
sources.debtQuadrant: Reckless or prudent, deliberate or inadvertent: not all technical debt is the same.
sources.cunningham: The original debt metaphor: shipping early is fine if you pay it back by refactoring.
sources.pciDss: The card industry's security standard: what changes when you store, process or transmit card data.
sources.model: Our own estimates. They show the direction and rough size of an effect, never a measurement.
sources.accelerate: Delivery performance research: small batches, loose coupling and fast feedback predict outcomes.
sources.microservicePremium: Microservices carry a cost premium that only pays off past a certain complexity.
sources.richardson: Sagas, database per service and the patterns that replace distributed transactions.
sources.helland: Why systems at scale give up distributed transactions and design for uncertainty instead.
sources.wardley: Map components by evolution: build what differentiates you, buy what has become a commodity.
sources.feathers: Legacy code is code without tests; seams are where you change it safely.
sources.strangler: Replace a system gradually by growing the new one around the old until it can be removed.
sources.sre: Error budgets, toil and reliability as a feature with a cost.

reversibility.title: Checkout needs to take money
reversibility.concept: Reversibility: one-way and two-way doors, and the last responsible moment.
reversibility.voice: Three engineers, one database, zero regrets. So far.
reversibility.briefing: Launch is in six weeks and nobody has written a line of payments code. Some of the ways in are easy to walk back out of. One is not.
reversibility.dilemma: How does the money get in, and which of these doors can you walk back through?
reversibility.disagreement: Experts disagree here. Some argue a port is cheap insurance; others call a one-implementation interface speculative generality. Both are right in some company.
reversibility.readNext: Start with the 'one-way door' passage of the 2015 Amazon letter, then the last responsible moment, then write your first real ADR in Nygard's format.

hosted-checkout.title: Hosted checkout, wired into the monolith
hosted-checkout.optimizes: Launch in two weeks, with card data kept off your servers.
hosted-checkout.costs: A fee on every order; their checkout page, not yours; and leaving later means migrating customers and contracts.

payments-port.title: A payments module behind a port
payments-port.costs: One extra week; an abstraction with exactly one implementation.

own-service.title: Own payments-service and ledger
own-service.optimizes: Control of the payment flow and the margin, and a ledger of your own from day one.
own-service.costs: The whole six weeks; card data in scope. A one-way door.

events.processor-outage: Saturday, 14:10. The card processor is down for two hours.
events.first-friday-rush: First Friday rush. Checkout slows to a crawl after 18:00.

inspections.checkout-fridays: Site inspection: checkout district congested every Friday after 18:00. Not yet a problem. Noted, in pencil.

review.which-door: Which part of this decision is a one-way door, and which part could you walk back?
review.what-given-up: What did you give up, and who pays for it?
review.when-revisit: What would make you revisit this, and how would you know?

rubric.grounded-context: The context names the constraints that actually shaped the choice (team, traffic, runway, deadline).
rubric.names-reversibility: The decision says how hard it is to undo.
rubric.names-tradeoff: The consequences name at least one force that got worse, not only the ones that got better.
rubric.names-given-up: What was given up is written down in a full sentence.
rubric.revisit-trigger: The revisit trigger is a condition someone could notice, not a hope.
